blocks.text:
I've set up a draft scenario for measles in Kenya. Please check these settings before I fetch the country data:

| Setting | Value | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Model | SEIR (lifelong immunity, so no return to susceptible) | Database: immunity is lifelong after infection or two doses |
| R0 | 15 | Database consensus 12–18. Single studies range from 6.95 (a primary-school outbreak in a partly vaccinated population) to 103.5 (a serology and surveillance review of urban African and Indian populations) |
| Latent period | 12 days | Database typical; consensus 7–21 days, single studies 10–16 |
| Infectious period | 8 days | CDC; every estimate in the database is 8 days |
| Case fatality ratio | 1.5% | Systematic review range 0.5–6%. The extremes are 0.1% (general population) and 29% (infants with intense exposure in an urban community), so CFR in low-resource settings is a major sensitivity |
| Agents / duration | 10,000 agents, 1 year | Default |
| Network | Random for now; becomes age-structured with Kenya's Prem 2021 matrix once demographics are fetched | |
| Seeding | Default 0.05% of agents | Default |

**Planned data fetches**
- **UN World Population Prospects for Kenya:** age structure, births, deaths and total population.
- **WHO/UNICEF measles vaccination coverage for Kenya:** this adds a vaccine entry at the reported coverage. Coverage is what decides whether an outbreak happens at all with R0 ≈ 15, because the herd-immunity threshold is about 93%.

**Questions on scope**
- **Area:** whole country, or a county such as Nairobi or a northern ASAL county where coverage tends to be lower? If you pick a county, ages, contacts and coverage stay national.
- **Exploration:** do you want to compare R0 12 against 18, or a reactive campaign against the baseline?

blocks.text:
The data is applied. Here is the final setup:

**Demographics (UN World Population Prospects 2024)**
- **Population:** 58.6 million.
- **Age structure:** 43.9% under 18, 53.1% aged 18–64, 3% aged 65 and over.
- **Births and deaths:** about 27.1 births and 7.2 deaths per 1,000 people per year, so new unvaccinated people are added throughout the run.
- **Contacts:** the network is now age-structured, using Kenya's Prem 2021 contact matrix. Beta was recalculated so R0 stays at 15. No literature warnings came back.

**Vaccination (WHO/UNICEF estimates, 2025)**
- **Reported coverage:** first dose 80%, second dose 81%.
- **What the model uses:** 80% of people start immune on day 0, with no campaign during the run. This is a simplification. The database has no vaccine efficacy, so every vaccinated person is treated as fully protected. Real immunity is lower because one dose works about 93% of the time, coverage differs by age group, and unvaccinated people cluster in some communities. So this setup probably **understates** how many people can still catch measles.
- **Data check:** second-dose coverage being higher than first-dose coverage is odd, because hardly anyone can get the second dose without the first. It usually points to denominator or reporting problems in administrative data.

**What to expect**
- With 80% immune, the effective reproduction number at the start is about 15 × 0.2 ≈ 3. That is well above 1, so expect a large outbreak among the 20% who are not immune.
- Births keep adding susceptible people, which matters if you later run this for several years.

**Choice of mode**
- **Recommendation:** run as agents (simulated individual people). Nothing in this setup depends on chance, so the compartmental model would give essentially the same epidemic.
- **What agents add:** fade-out by chance, uncertainty bands if you add replicates, and room for heterogeneity later.
- **What the compartmental model offers:** one exact average curve, the R0 formula exactly, and the same result every time.
- **Run size:** at 10,000 agents each agent stands for about 5,900 people, so the default seeding is a few thousand initial infections nationally.

blocks.text:
Run 1 is a worst case: almost everyone who was not immune at the start got infected.

**What happened**
- **Size:** 19.3% of Kenyans were infected over the year. That is nearly all of the 20% who started without immunity, plus a share of newborns. With an effective reproduction number of about 3 at the start, the final-size equation predicts about 94% of those susceptible people get infected, and the run matches that.
- **Peak:** day 94, with about 1.7 million people infected at the same time.
- **Deaths:** about 170,000. This is the 1.5% case fatality ratio applied to every case, so the CFR's range (0.5–6% in the review) changes this number roughly in proportion.
- **R0:** 15 as calibrated. Starsim's own estimate agrees at 14.99, but this is a run as agents, so treat R0 as approximate.

**Why this overstates a real Kenyan outbreak**
Real Kenyan measles outbreaks are far smaller than this. The biggest reasons:
1. **Where immunity sits.** The 80% immunity is spread evenly across all ages. In reality most adults are immune from past infection, and susceptible people are concentrated in under-5s and in pockets of low coverage. So 20% of adults are wrongly counted as susceptible here, and the pool of susceptible people is too big.
2. **No geography.** The contact network mixes the whole country. Real transmission is limited by distance, so outbreaks stay local (in ASAL counties, informal settlements and refugee camps) instead of spreading nationwide at once.
3. **Seeding.** The default seeding starts about 29,000 people infected on day 0 across the country, which is far from a single introduction. This brings the peak earlier, though it barely changes the final size.
4. **No response.** There is no reactive campaign, no supplementary immunisation activity (SIA), and nobody changes behaviour as cases rise.
5. **One replicate.** There are no uncertainty bands.

**Suggested next steps**
- **Fix the baseline first.** Either use a smaller area with a realistic number of initial cases, or add `rel_sus_cv`, which gives people different levels of susceptibility so the most susceptible are infected first. Its value would be an illustrative assumption, not a database figure.
- **Then compare interventions.** Test a reactive vaccination campaign against this baseline. Its coverage and 90% efficacy would also be illustrative assumptions.

blocks.text:
The reactive campaign (Run 2) cut infections and deaths by about two thirds compared with Run 1. The only change between the runs is the campaign: 70% coverage and 90% efficacy from day 30 to day 60. Both numbers are illustrative assumptions, not database values.

| | Run 1 (no campaign) | Run 2 (campaign) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Peak infections | 1.74 M | 0.50 M | −71% |
| Peak day | 94 | 65 | 29 days earlier |
| Total infected | 11.3 M (19.3%) | 4.2 M (7.2%) | −7.1 M (−63%) |
| Deaths | 170,000 | 58,600 | −111,000 (−66%) |

**How to read it**
- **Why the peak comes earlier.** The campaign cut the rise short: once enough susceptible people were vaccinated, the effective reproduction number fell below 1 and the epidemic turned around on day 65. That is not an epidemic speeding up.
- **What the doses bought.** The campaign gave 41.6 million doses, offered to everyone whether already vaccinated or not. With 80% already immune, most of those doses went to people who were protected anyway. Only about one in five reached someone susceptible. That works out to roughly 160 infections averted per 1,000 doses.
- **What this suggests.** A campaign aimed at under-5s or at the counties with the lowest coverage would probably avert most of these infections with far fewer doses. That is the question worth testing next with an age-limited campaign (`age_max`).
- **What it could not prevent.** The roughly 4 million infections left are mostly those that happened before and during days 30–60, while protection was still building. Starting earlier is the main lever.

**Why these numbers are still too high**
Run 1's caveats still apply to both runs: immunity is spread evenly across ages, the country mixes as one population, the national seeding is large, and there is one replicate with no bands. Read the absolute numbers as inflated. The relative effect of the campaign is the more robust finding.

input.title: Measles in Kenya: unmitigated outbreak vs. reactive vaccination campaign (SEIR, agent-based, 1 year)
input.meaning:
Run 1 (baseline, no response) shows the immunity gap in Kenya. With R0 around 15 and 80% immune at the start, the effective reproduction number is about 3, and the outbreak runs until it has used up nearly all the susceptible people, as the final-size equation predicts. Deaths follow directly from the assumed 1.5% case fatality ratio, so they scale with the CFR across the review's 0.5–6% range.

Run 2 adds a reactive mass campaign starting on day 30, when about 1% of agents had been infected. Compared with Run 1:
- The epidemic turns around earlier, because the campaign pushes the effective reproduction number below 1 while the curve is still rising. The earlier peak reflects a truncated rise, not faster spread.
- Total infections and deaths fall by about two thirds, and the peak falls by more than two thirds.
- Most of the infections that remain happened before or during the campaign window, while protection was building. The start date is therefore the main lever on how much the campaign can avert.
- The campaign was untargeted, so with 80% already immune only about one dose in five reached a susceptible person. Restricting it by age or place would likely keep most of the benefit with a much smaller campaign.

The recorded R0 (about 15) is approximate, as in any run as agents. It is the baseline value: the run does not report the effective reproduction number after vaccination.
input.summary: This scenario models a national measles outbreak in Kenya with literature-consensus parameters (R0 15, 12-day latent period, 8-day infectious period, 1.5% case fatality ratio), UN population data, Kenya's Prem 2021 contact matrix, and WHO/UNICEF 2025 first-dose coverage (80%) treated as immunity at the start. With R0 near 15, 80% immunity is well below the herd-immunity threshold of about 93%, so the effective reproduction number at the start is about 3. Without a response, nearly all of the remaining susceptible people are infected within the year (Run 1). A reactive campaign from day 30 to day 60 (Run 2: 70% coverage, 90% efficacy, both illustrative) cuts infections and deaths by about two thirds and ends the epidemic about a month earlier. The campaign was offered to everyone regardless of vaccination status, so most doses went to people who were already immune; targeting by age or place is the obvious way to get more effect per dose. Both runs overstate absolute numbers because immunity is spread evenly across ages and the whole country mixes as one population. Read the relative effect of the campaign as the more robust result. These are illustrative scenarios, not forecasts.
input.next_steps:
- Make the baseline realistic: restrict to a high-risk county (e.g. an ASAL county or Nairobi informal settlements) with its own population and a small realistic seed (e.g. 10 cases).
- Add variation in susceptibility between people (rel_sus_cv) as an illustrative brake, or fit it to an observed attack rate from a recent Kenyan outbreak while keeping R0 fixed.
- Targeting: compare an under-18 (or under-5) campaign with the mass campaign, using delivered doses as the measure of cost.
- Timing: rerun with campaign start days 10, 30 and 60 to show the cost of delay.
- Sensitivity: R0 12 vs 18 and CFR 0.5% vs 6%; add replicates (within the 500,000 agent-year cap) to get uncertainty bands.
- Longer horizon: a multi-year run to see susceptible people building up through births at current coverage and when outbreaks recur.
- Data to check: subnational MCV1/MCV2 coverage and serosurveys for Kenya, recent outbreak line lists (KEMRI, MoH, WHO AFRO), and the dates and coverage of past supplementary immunisation activities (SIAs).
input.limitations:
- Immunity at the start: WHO/UNICEF MCV1 coverage (80%) was applied as immunity at day 0, spread evenly across all ages, and assumed fully protective. In reality most adults are immune through past infection, susceptible people are concentrated in young children and low-coverage communities, and one-dose efficacy is below 100%. This puts too many susceptible people among adults and inflates the outbreak.
- Data quality: the 2025 estimates show MCV2 (81%) above MCV1 (80%), which is implausible and suggests problems with administrative denominators.
- Mixing: the population mixes by age through a national contact matrix but is otherwise homogeneous, with no geography, counties, urban/rural structure, refugee camps or travel. Real Kenyan outbreaks are local and much smaller.
- Seeding: the default seeding (0.05% of agents, tens of thousands of people nationally on day 0) is far from a realistic introduction. It brings the epidemic forward in time, though it hardly changes the final size.
- Single pathogen. No behaviour change in response to the epidemic, no case isolation, contact tracing or routine catch-up during the year, and no reduced transmission from hospital care.
- Fatality: one case fatality ratio (1.5%, database typical) applied to all ages. The literature spans 0.5–6%, and measles CFR is much higher in infants, malnourished children and crisis settings. Fatality by age was not modelled.
- Illustrative assumptions: the campaign's coverage (70%), efficacy (90%, leaky) and timing (days 30–60) are illustrative, not from the database. The default latent-period spread (gamma, sd 3.5 days) and infectious-period spread (gamma, sd 2.4 days) are model defaults.
- Run size and uncertainty: 10,000 agents (about 5,900 people per agent), one replicate each, so no uncertainty bands. Runs are illustrative scenarios, not forecasts.

blocks.text:
I've written the report comparing Run 1 (no response) and Run 2 (reactive campaign). You can download it as HTML, Markdown, Word or PDF from the Report section of the Dashboard.

It explains why the outbreak is so large, says the campaign's relative effect is the more reliable finding, and lists the limits. The main ones are:
- Immunity is spread evenly across ages and assumed to work in everyone.
- The whole country mixes as one population, with no geography.
- Many people are infected on day 0.
- The campaign's coverage, efficacy and timing are illustrative assumptions.
- Each run is a single replicate, so there are no uncertainty bands.

The next steps it suggests are to run one high-risk county with a small number of initial cases, compare campaigns limited by age and started on different days, and test the range of R0 and case fatality ratio.
